records.summary: The idea is a service for company monitoring and structured registry data across connected European registries. It would provide company, ownership, financial, and registry-event information to compliance, research, and business-intelligence teams. The proposed moat is entity resolution and daily synchronization across countries.
records.how_money: Firmium lists Professional from €250/user/month and Data API from €490/month; both have a 12-month minimum. Other providers list paid subscriptions and API plans.
records.market: Germany, Austria, and Switzerland (DACH), with the sources also describing connected European registries.

revenue_claims.claim: Eurostat counts 3,185,294 German and 602,763 Austrian enterprises in 2023; Swiss statistics report 610,000 market-economy enterprises in 2021.

records.paid_demand: Providers list paid plans, including Firmium from €250/user/month and GlobalEntity from €19/user/month. The sources found no verified revenue or paying-user counts; listed prices are not proof of completed sales.

competitors.name: Firmium
competitors.note: Paid plans have a 12-month minimum; it also advertises free company profiles and daily synchronization.

competitors.name: GlobalEntity
competitors.note: Its documentation lists Germany, Austria, and Switzerland, plus ownership and monitoring features.

competitors.name: Global Database Regis
competitors.note: API general availability announced on 24 Jul 2026.

competitors.name: North Data
competitors.note: Advertises daily updates across many countries.

competitors.name: OpenCorporates
competitors.note: Essentials plan covers up to 500 API calls/month.

rounds.plain: K0 means the moat is too weak to take 3+ months to copy; the broad graph has no demonstrated advantage over existing providers. K2 means two or more competing launches within six months: Global Database Regis and GlobalEntity fall in the cited window.

The earlier kill-check considered the cross-registry data asset defensible and found only one dated competing launch in its search. Later evidence identified GlobalEntity and Global Database Regis launches in the same window, superseding that result.

risks: Registry access and reuse terms differ by country.
No verified revenue, customer count, churn, or paying-user evidence was found.
The proposed ≤5 h/week operating limit is unverified.
The broad build requires source-rights mapping, connectors, normalization, entity matching, history, and correction handling.
records.moat: A compiled-data moat could come from reliable cross-border entity resolution, ownership links, and dated change history. It is weak in the broad form described: the underlying records are public or reusable, and Firmium, North Data, and GlobalEntity already offer overlapping data, monitoring, or synchronization.

hours.note: The limit is not demonstrated; no operating business or time log exists.

records.next_steps: In one workday, compare a real cross-border company group across Firmium and GlobalEntity. Record provenance, ownership links, event history, freshness, API/export limits, and price; proceed only if there is a repeatable buyer-critical gap.

rounds.plain: K0 means the moat is too weak to take 3+ months to copy; free public source data and existing vendors leave little demonstrated differentiation. K2 means two or more competing launches within six months; the cited launches include Registrum's endpoint and Global Database Regis.

The earlier kill-check judged the parsed account and ownership data a months-to-copy asset and found no direct launch. Later evidence identified CompanyStack as an exact competitor and documented recent releases, superseding that result.

risks: No verified revenue, churn, or paying-customer evidence was found.
Companies House data is free and available through an API.
Only 2.0% of active companies' latest accounts showed turnover as of 4 Oct 2026, according to CompanyStack.
CompanyStack says its health score has not been statistically tested against company failures.
The ≤5-hour weekly operating limit is not supported by public evidence.
records.moat: Parsed accounts, ownership links, and source dates could form a maintained data asset, but it is not exclusive. The sources name several providers with overlapping financial histories, ownership data, screening, or monitoring; CompanyStack already covers the proposed core product.

hours.note: The limit is unverified; expect more founder involvement during build, launch, and data incidents.

records.next_steps: Within one workday, build a sample screen for one specific buyer workflow from public filings and offer a clearly described paid pilot at the £29/month CompanyStack API Starter price point. Treat a paid pilot, not a waitlist signup, as the pass signal.

records.summary: The idea is an API and webhook service that checks customer product catalogs against recall records and sends matches. It would serve retailers, marketplaces, and inventory software providers. The sources describe a possible data and switching-cost moat, but say it is weak today and cite recent competing launches.
records.how_money: recallsapi.com lists Starter at $29/month, Growth at $79/month, and Scale at $199/month. Other listed offers include per-match pricing and subscriptions.
records.customer: Retailers, marketplaces, and inventory software providers.
records.market: The lead documents US agency data; the sources say state and non-US recalls are out of scope and some feeds are not yet connected.

revenue_claims.claim: The European Commission recorded 4,671 Safety Gate alerts and 5,794 follow-up actions for 2025.
CPSC reported 542 recalls and safety warnings issued in 2025.
More than 75,000 independent sellers exceeded $1 million in Amazon's store in 2025.

records.paid_demand: recallsapi.com lists plans from $29/month, but the sources found no verified customer revenue or paid conversion. RecallGuard lists $0.10 per match and documents an operator self-test, not customer revenue.

competitors.name: recallsapi.com
competitors.note: Lists daily checked recall matches across customer catalogs.

competitors.name: Recalert
competitors.price: $29/month for up to 500 SKUs; $99/month for up to 10,000 SKUs

competitors.name: RecallDash
competitors.note: Square sync or CSV where available.

competitors.name: RecallGuard
competitors.note: Docs report an operator self-test, not customer revenue; webhook route returned 404.

competitors.name: RecallDocket
competitors.note: Third-party listing says the app is unavailable and shows zero reviews; listing reports launch on May 19, 2026.

competitors.name: RecallMatching
competitors.note: Early access; launch date unverified.

competitors.name: Covala
competitors.note: API by request; price unverified.

competitors.name: Oredrift EU Recall API
competitors.note: EU Safety Gate API.

rounds.plain: K0 means the moat is too weak to take 3+ months to copy; there is no evidenced shared correction corpus or network effect. K2 means two or more competing launches within six months; the sources cite RecallDocket and RecallGuard.

The earlier kill-check judged the multi-agency corpus, matching, and catalog history to be a growing data asset and found only one dated recent direct launch. Later evidence identified RecallDocket and RecallGuard, superseding that result.

risks: No verified customer revenue, churn, retention, subscriber count, installations, or paid conversion was found.
The underlying US agency data is public and reproducible; state and non-US recalls are out of scope in the documented coverage.
False negatives, stale feeds, or overstated match claims could cause customer harm; the sources say a match needs review and no match is not a safety certification.
The ≤5 h/week operating limit is unverified.
The listed competitor app RecallDocket is unavailable and has zero reviews, so its current offer is weak evidence.
records.moat: Potentially, normalized identifiers, confidence explanations, source freshness, catalog monitoring, and retained match history could create data and switching-cost advantages. The sources say the current moat is weak: public-domain records are easy to obtain, competitors already match recalls, and no shared correction corpus or network effect is evidenced.

hours.note: Unverified; plausible only for a narrow self-serve product after stable automation.

records.next_steps: In one workday, check buyer-intent terms in Google Keyword Planner and replay sample product barcodes against official recall records, manually inspecting candidate matches. This tests search demand and basic match quality, not willingness to pay.
